That pointer table is the hinge of the whole design: the CUDA kernels never see a Python-side index, they read block ids from the metadata buffer and address the KV pools directly, which is why the same kernel handles any batch composition without recompilation.

Attention then proceeds in blocks. AtomBuilder derives per-head work atoms — fixed-size query-and-key spans — from the batch metadata, and the module calls BlockedFlashAttn with those atoms, out scratch, and the pointer tables; its call signature at line 88 is worth reading as the specification of the whole ragged layout. The sizes are tuned by get_q_block_size per head dimension. The same pattern frames both ends of the network: RaggedEmbeddingKernel gathers embedding rows for the packed token stream, and RaggedLogitsGather copies only the last-token rows of each sequence out for sampling — the unembed GEMM still runs over every hidden state, but the gather that produces logits touches the minimum.

Policies, containers, and a metaclass that checks your weights

Getting a Llama checkpoint into this layout is the job of the policy layer. InferenceV2Policy declares two responsibilities — build_model at line 140 instantiates the model class, and populate_model_parameters at line 189 routes every incoming tensor to the right destination through a ContainerMap that separates transformer-layer containers from the embedding-side one. A metaclass enforces the contract: LayerMetaclass rewrites class construction so that annotated attributes become parameter slots, and its call override at line 150 refuses half-initialized containers — a checkpoint loader cannot silently leave a layer empty. Weights themselves are wrapped as InferenceParameter, a tensor subclass that tracks device residency so a quantized weight still living on CPU is caught at use time rather than at a mysterious kernel crash.

The concrete pair for this tour is the Llama family. Llama2Policy supplies the model class and its container map; Llama2TransformerContainer and Llama2NonTransformerContainer name the per-layer and global weights. The model’s forward at line 199 is refreshingly literal: _forward_embed, then a Python loop calling _forward_transformer_layer once per layer index, then _forward_unembed. All the cleverness is one level down, in DSTransformerModelBase, whose factory methods — make_embedding_layer at line 303, make_qkv_layer at line 363, make_norm_layer at line 579 — consult per-architecture configuration, and whose maybe_allocate_kv at line 436 asks the state manager for blocks before each pass using get_kv_requirements. A sibling base, DSMoETransformerModelBase, adds expert layers through make_moe_layer for Mixtral and Qwen-MoE checkpoints.

DSModules: every organ is swappable

The most transferable idea in the tree is the module contract. DSModuleBase requires each implementation to name itself and answer supports_config — a predicate saying which configurations it can handle. Registration is self-service: subclassing DSModuleRegistryBase enrolls the class via register_module at line 49, so importing an implementation file is enough to make it discoverable. At engine construction, the heuristic pickers — instantiate_attention at line 36, instantiate_linear at line 75, instantiate_pre_norm at line 158, plus their embed, unembed, and MoE siblings — walk the registered implementations in priority order and take the first that supports the requested configuration. The shipped set shows the spectrum: DSDenseBlockedAttention builds atoms with build_atoms at line 139 before its forward at line 152; BlasFPLinear is the honest pure-GEMM fallback for unquantized weights; DSPreRMSCUDAModule fuses RMSNorm; DSRaggedEmbedding and DSRaggedUnembed bracket the stream. Anyone adding a model family follows a documented recipe — the AddingAModel guide in the same folder — and anyone adding a faster kernel only has to satisfy the same config predicate, which is exactly how this tree wants extensions to arrive.

From Install to Your First Model

Install with pip install deepspeed, then the v2 path is three lines of Python: from deepspeed.inference.v2.engine_factory import build_hf_engine; engine = build_hf_engine("meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf"); engine.put(0, tokens). Between those lines, the factory loads the checkpoint streaming class, builds the policy, populates every container, wraps the model in InferenceEngineV2, and returns an object whose put/query/flush verbs are the entire API. Be honest about the fine print, because the code is: the v2 engine is marked experimental in its own docs, the blocked CUDA kernels target NVIDIA tensor-core GPUs, and running with tensor parallelism greater than one is the configuration the engine actually exercises — single-GPU mode works through the BLAS linear module but is not the optimized path. Quantized-weight support exists in the cutlass GEMM kernels but the coverage of bit-widths is narrower than the training side’s optimizer zoo, and there is no continuous-batching scheduler loop shipped as a runnable daemon — the engine provides put/query/can_schedule and expects your serving loop to call them, unlike the turnkey HTTP servers this series has met in lmdeploy and local inference servers. What you get in exchange is the clearest executable specification of ragged serving we have read: four trees of code where every tensor has a declared owner. Compare the training half at our first DeepSpeed tour, the quantized-kernel approach of Triton, the execution-plan machinery of ONNX Runtime, the mobile side of ExecuTorch, and the speech sibling faster-whisper — the same lesson repeats: production inference is bookkeeping with arithmetic inside.
entry.summary: A second source tour of microsoft/DeepSpeed, this time through the inference half of the tree: the v2 engine factory and its put/query scheduling surface, the ragged manager that tracks sequences in block-sized KV pools, the RaggedBatchWrapper that packs variable-length requests into one CUDA-shaped batch, the policy and container machinery that loads Llama checkpoints without PyTorch modules, and the DSModule registry that swaps every transformer organ for a fused kernel.

entry.title: From Export to Bare Metal - The .pte Path Through pytorch/executorch

link.title: From Export to Bare Metal - The .pte Path Through pytorch/executorch

entry.content:
Every framework we have toured in this series — Triton for kernels, vLLM for throughput, MLC for cross-platform compilation — assumes you have an operating system, a Python runtime, and memory to spare. ExecuTorch, PyTorch’s edge sibling, drops all three assumptions: its target machines are microcontrollers, DSPs, and phone NPUs where your whole model must fit into a memory budget you declare in advance. The price of that constraint shapes every file in the repository, and it produces one of the cleanest ideas in inference engineering: the allocation plan is computed at export time, on a machine that has plenty of RAM, and shipped inside the artifact itself. The runtime never allocates a tensor at inference — it replays a script. This tour follows a .pte file end to end: the exir export flow that partitions, plans, and serializes it; the loader that memory-maps it; the Method that executes it one step at a time; the backend contract that hands subgraphs to vendor libraries; and the LLM runner that turns all of it into a chat loop. As always, this is an educational read of published source on the main branch, under the BSD-style license.

What makes the design worth studying is how much it refuses to do at runtime. There is no scheduler, no batcher, no memory arena hunting for blocks mid-inference — all of that was decided by a Python pass with the whole graph in view. The C++ side stays small enough to read in an afternoon, which is exactly the point for software that ships inside hearing aids and drones.

Overview of the .pte path: exir partitioners carve subgraphs to backends, the memory-planning pass assigns every tensor a spec, serialize_for_executorch writes the flatbuffer, Program loads it, Method replays the plan through the BackendInterface, and the Module plus LLM runner wrap it into an application.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • partitioner.py defines the abstract Partitioner whose call at line 66 runs partition at 75 and returns a PartitionResult with lowered subgraphs.
  • memory_planning_pass.py is where allocation becomes data: MemoryPlanningPass runs at line 280 with a multi-method variant at 346.
  • memory_planning.py computes lifetimes with update_all_tensors_lifetime and validates them through verify_storage_reuse at 165.
  • _serialize.py is the exit door: serialize_for_executorch writes the flatbuffer program and its external data segments.
  • program.cpp is the loader: Program::load verifies the file, num_methods at 353 counts entry points, and load_method at 384 builds a Method.
  • method_meta.cpp reports what a method needs — input shapes, output shapes, memory plan sizes.
  • method.cpp is the engine: Method::init wires kernels and delegates once, step at 1723 and execute at 1780 replay the plan.
  • interface.h is the vendor contract: BackendInterface with init at 84 and execute at 99.
  • module.cpp is the friendly C++ API: Module::load picks a DataLoader strategy, load_method at 543 prepares an entry point.
  • text_llm_runner.cpp is a complete chat loop: generate drives prefill at 284 and per-token decode.
  • text_decoder_runner.cpp runs one method step per token through the sampler.
  • memory_allocator.h and hierarchical_allocator.h are the bump allocators that hold every planned buffer.

Export: edge dialect, delegates, and a plan for every byte

The Python half of the repo answers a question most runtimes answer with heuristics at load time: how much memory does this model need, and where does each tensor sit? The flow starts with torch.export and a descent into the edge dialect — operator decompositions that rewrite ATen ops into the edge subset with explicit dtype and layout. Then partitioning: a backend implements the Partitioner interface, declares which ops it supports, and the exporter slices matching subgraphs out of the graph, wrapping each in a lowered module that the backend compiles however it likes. Whatever the backend cannot claim stays as a portable-kernel subgraph, so a Core ML or QNN delegate can sit beside reference C++ kernels in the same method.

The distinctive part is the planning pass. MemoryPlanningPass walks the traced graph, and for every node that materializes a tensor it attaches an allocation spec at line 229 — size, dtype, alignment, and a lifetime computed from when the tensor is last read. The core machinery in memory_planning.py collects specs from nodes, then solves a two-dimensional packing problem: tensors whose lifetimes do not overlap can share one buffer, and update_all_tensors_lifetime at line 548 supplies the intervals the packer needs. The result is a set of named memory plans — each a fixed-size pool with fixed offsets — and a verifier at line 165 that refuses to emit a program whose planned buffers overlap in invalid ways. Serialization then writes the whole story into the .pte: the flatbuffer program from serialize_for_executorch at line 44 plus constant segments laid out so a device can consume them directly. It is the same precompute-everything philosophy we saw in ONNX Runtime’s planners in the onnxruntime-2 tour, taken to its logical endpoint: not cached per input signature, but baked into the file.

Loading: segments, verification, and zero-copy

The C++ half begins with Program::load, and its first act is paranoia. The loader checks the flatbuffer identifier, verifies the whole buffer with a flatbuffers verifier, parses the extended header, and only then hands back a Program. The file is organized as segments — program, constants, mutable data — described by segment info records, and the loader never copies them: it keeps a pointer into whatever the DataLoader provided, which can be a file read, an mmap, or memory embedded at link time. PteDataMap indexes the named data so constants land where the plan expects. A Program can hold several methods — the LLM use case compiles prefill and decode as separate entry points — enumerated by num_methods at line 353 and get_method_name at 364, each loaded independently through load_method at 384, which consults method_meta for the shapes and plan sizes it must reserve.

Execution: one method, one step, one delegate call

Method::init at line 937 is where the plan meets real memory. The caller supplies a hierarchical allocator — a stack of named pools sized exactly as the export promised — and init carves every planned buffer out of those pools without a single dynamic allocation. It then walks the graph’s instructions: portable kernels are resolved by name against the registered kernel library, and each delegated subgraph is initialized through the backend’s init at line 84, which compiles the subgraph into an opaque DelegateHandle. From there, execution is a replay: Method::step at line 1723 copies inputs into their planned slots, execute at 1780 walks the instruction list — kernel calls through the EValue variant, or execute at line 99 on the backend for delegated spans — and every write lands in memory whose address was decided in Python. The TensorParser is the quiet workhorse mapping feed tensors onto the planned buffers, and the optional EventTracer records per-op spans when profiling is compiled in. The Module layer above smooths the ergonomics — its constructors at line 125 choose between FileDataLoader and mmap variants depending on the platform — and BundledModule goes one step further by linking the .pte into the application binary itself, which is how a watch face model ships with no filesystem at all.

Two supporting pieces make this machinery survivable on real hardware. The first is the DataLoader abstraction: because the loader only ever hands out borrowed views — the FreeableBuffer type wraps a pointer plus a destructor — the same Method code runs against a heap read on a laptop and against flash-mapped memory on an RTOS without caring which. The Module constructors pick the strategy per platform, trying mmap first and falling back to file reads where it is unavailable. The second is the Result type, which replaces exceptions with a value-or-error pattern throughout the runtime: every loader call, init call, and step returns one, and the absence of exception machinery keeps the binary small enough for the MCUs this code targets. Neither piece is glamorous, but together they are why the executor compiles with almost no standard library dependency — an explicit design goal you can feel in every header.

From Install to Your First Model

The LLM path ties the pieces together. TextLLMRunner owns two methods from one .pte — prefill and decode — and generate at line 74 runs prefill at 284 in chunks sized to the device, then loops TextDecoderRunner::step at line 40, which executes the decode method once, samples, appends the token, and invokes the callback. Nothing here batches across users — the whole design targets one conversation on one device, which is why the runner can stay a few hundred lines.

After pip install executorch, the knobs worth knowing are the memory ones: memory-planning modes choose between contiguous pools and per-plan pools, --memory-planning output can be inspected as a text layout, and backends like XNNPACK or Core ML register themselves as partitioners you add to the export call. Honest limits: we read the loader and method hot path, not the kernel libraries or the vendor delegates — the QNN and Core ML trees are large projects of their own. We benchmarked nothing; the zero-copy claims are structural, and real devices add alignment surprises that the dim-order passes only partially hide. And the executor is single-threaded by design — parallelism exists only inside backends. Compared with OpenVINO and ONNX Runtime, which carry their allocators and schedulers into the runtime, ExecuTorch’s answer is radical precomputation: the .pte is not just a model format, it is a memory map — and that is why the smallest devices in this series run it.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of pytorch/executorch along the whole life of a .pte file: the exir partitioners and memory-planning pass that pre-compute every tensor's address at export time, the serialized flatbuffer with its segments, Program's zero-copy loader, Method's init-once execute-per-step loop, the BackendInterface delegate contract, and the Module and LLM runner layers on top.

entry.title: Inside the Seek Loop - Timestamps, Fallback, and Hallucination Guards in SYSTRAN/faster-whisper

link.title: Inside the Seek Loop - Timestamps, Fallback, and Hallucination Guards in SYSTRAN/faster-whisper

entry.content:
Our first walk of SYSTRAN/faster-whisper introduced the cast: WhisperModel, the batched wrapper, PyAV audio, the Silero VAD, and the claim that a reimplementation on CTranslate2 makes the same model four times faster. What that tour did not open up is transcribe.py’s engine room — the eighteen hundred lines where the actual decoding decisions live. Whisper’s own implementation is famously a pile of heuristics: a seek pointer that sometimes advances and sometimes retries, three separate tests for whether a decoded window can be trusted, a prompt manager that keeps context coherent across windows, and a timestamp alignment scheme that reads cross-attention maps. faster-whisper rebuilds every one of those heuristics in Python over CTranslate2’s primitives, and reading them is a masterclass in production speech recognition. As always, this is an educational read of published source on the master branch, MIT-licensed; the first post covers the module map we now zoom past.

The one-sentence summary: generate_segments is a clock, generate_with_fallback is a skeptic, and the VAD is the map that tells both where speech actually is. Everything else in the package exists to feed, verify, or measure that trio.

Overview of the decoding machinery: the package surface hands audio through the VAD into WhisperModel, whose seek loop and fallback logic drive CTranslate2; the batched wrapper reuses the same pieces over merged chunks, while benchmarks, tests, and the Docker entry measure and package it all.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • transcribe.py holds the whole engine: WhisperModel with its public transcribe at line 781.
  • The seek loop is generate_segments, and its clip arithmetic starts at line 1176.
  • generate_with_fallback decides whether a window’s output can be trusted.
  • add_word_timestamps rebuilds word timing from the align call at line 1746.
  • The batched wrapper is the batched sibling, with its own transcribe at line 254.
  • vad.py supplies get_speech_timestamps and collect_chunks at 220.
  • audio.py decodes any container through PyAV with decode_audio and pad_or_trim at 117.
  • utils.py fetches converted checkpoints via download_model and formats timestamps at line 118.
  • speed_benchmark.py measures real-time factor with measure_speed; wer_benchmark.py scores accuracy.

The seek loop: windows, clips, and silence

The public transcribe builds the option dataclasses — TranscriptionOptions at line 71 carries every knob — and then hands you a generator, which is where generate_segments begins. Its unit of work is the thirty-second window. Without a VAD, the seek pointer marches through the file in 30-second steps; with one, the loop first asks get_speech_timestamps for speech regions and converts them into seek clips, so the pointer jumps from speech to speech and silence never reaches the model. The per-window bookkeeping is precise: time_offset at line 1205 converts the seek index into seconds via the feature extractor’s per-frame time, the mel features are sliced to the window, and everything decoded is stamped relative to that offset. After a window is accepted, the seek advances past the last timestamp token rather than the full window — the original Whisper’s trick for not losing audio between timestamp boundaries.

The most interesting branch is the hallucination guard. Whisper’s known failure mode is inventing fluent text over silence or music — famously “Thank you for watching” loops. When hallucination_silence_threshold is set and a segment looks suspicious, the code at lines 1327 through 1369 uses the word timestamps to find where speech actually resumed, truncates the seek to the last real word end, and re-decodes just the silence-free remainder. Note the dependency: the guard needs word timestamps to work, which is why the option is disabled by default and why the docstring ties the two together. The VAD path also patches timestamps back into wall-clock positions through SpeechTimestampsMap, because chunks were removed and re-ordered and every segment’s reported time must land in the original audio’s frame of reference.

generate_with_fallback: deciding a window is wrong

generate_with_fallback is the skeptic that sits between the encoder and your transcript. It samples with the first temperature, then runs three tests on the result. The first is repetitiveness: get_compression_ratio at line 1924 zlib-compresses the text, and if the ratio above the threshold says the output is too repetitive, needs_fallback is set at line 1520. The second is confidence: if the average log probability at line 1533 falls under log_prob_threshold, the window is rejected. The third is the clever one — if there is no speech in the window at all, the low-probability result is explicitly accepted at line 1550, because “silence” is a correct answer for silence, and punishing it would cause the fallback loop to hallucinate something to say. On failure, the temperature climbs — up to len(temperatures) retries, each with best_of sampling at line 1473 — and the best surviving candidate wins. Before any of this runs, get_suppressed_tokens at line 1929 assembles the suppression list: non-speech tokens, user-supplied suppressions, and the compression-ratio flagged set. The prompt machinery at line 1569 closes the loop across windows, extending the previous window’s text so the model keeps its style and vocabulary — sot_sequence and task tokens included.

Word timestamps: alignment from CTranslate2

Word timestamps in this codebase are not heuristic guesswork — they are cross-attention arithmetic delegated to CTranslate2. add_word_timestamps at line 1604 collects the text tokens per segment and calls find_alignment at line 1735, which invokes model.align at line 1746 — CTranslate2 runs the DTW over cross-attention maps with a median filter, and returns token-to-frame alignments plus per-token probabilities. The Python side then does the cleanup Whisper’s original is known for: a median-based duration cap at lines 1630 through 1653 truncates impossible word lengths at sentence boundaries, merge_punctuations at line 1955 glues punctuation back onto neighbors, and the tokenizer’s split_to_word_tokens handles scripts where words do not split on spaces — CJK among them. The same alignment data feeds the timestamp-based splitter at line 1061, which cuts long segments at reliable timestamp tokens when multilingual subtitles demand it, and detect_language at line 1811 reuses the encoder output for its language-likelihood pass.

The batched sibling and the VAD that feeds it

The speed story closes with the batched wrapper class at line 111. Its transcribe at line 254 asks the VAD for speech regions, then collect_chunks at line 220 reassembles them into batch_size windows of 30 seconds each — padding partial chunks — and forward at line 119 runs one CTranslate2 batch over all of them. Per-window decoding inside the batch is generate_segment_batched at line 174, which skips the fallback machinery for speed and returns logits-level results that the wrapper scores and trims at line 246. The results finally stream through _batched_segments_generator at line 582, where chunk offsets are restored to original-audio time — the same restore_speech_timestamps helper at line 1889 the non-batched path uses. The trade the README’s seventeen-seconds benchmark makes is now legible: batching and VAD pruning replace the fallback skeptic with a cheaper pass, and the Silero model itself at line 330 runs as a bundled ONNX file — the same runtime-engine pattern ONNX Runtime standardized, applied to a 2-megabyte gatekeeper.

Two support modules deserve their paragraph because both are quieter than they look. The feature extractor computes log-Mel spectrograms, and _get_feature_kwargs at line 763 quietly checks the model directory for a preprocessor config so that older converted checkpoints keep their original mel parameters instead of silently drifting — a two-line guard against one of the nastiest classes of silent accuracy bugs. The tokenizer wraps Hugging Face’s tokenizers library with Whisper’s task and language token bookkeeping, and its word-splitting logic is what makes CJK and mixed-script timestamps work at all. Around the package, the Docker entry point wires a wav file to a model with nothing but environment variables, and test_utils.py covers the download layer — including the resume-from-partial-download behavior that anyone on hotel Wi-Fi will eventually thank.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything above activates through arguments to transcribe(): vad_filter=True arms the VAD path, word_timestamps=True enables the alignment machinery, and hallucination_silence_threshold (a float in seconds) arms the guard — which requires word timestamps. The benchmark directory is the honest way to see the trade-offs: speed_benchmark.py sweeps model sizes and batch settings, memory_benchmark.py tracks peak memory per compute type, and wer_benchmark.py scores the accuracy cost of batching, with shared dataset helpers behind them.

Honest limits: this walk stayed in Python; the actual Transformer math is CTranslate2’s, and its align internals are a separate engine we did not read. The hallucination guard’s thresholds are heuristics tuned on English-ish audio — other languages may need different values, and the code itself warns that the timestamp trick assumes VAD quality. We read, not measured: the README’s numbers come from the benchmark files, not from us. And the fallback logic is deliberately conservative — turning all three guards off is a legitimate speed choice for clean single-speaker audio, as the tests in test_transcribe.py demonstrate with real fixtures. For context in this series: vLLM and SGLang batch text tokens across users, LocalAI and xorbitsai/inference wrap speech models behind the same server walls as LLMs, and OpenVINO quantizes the same Whisper architecture for CPU. faster-whisper’s lesson — guard the clock, trust the alignment, batch only what the VAD proves is speech — is the most transferable of the lot.
entry.summary: A second source tour of SYSTRAN/faster-whisper, this time inside the decoding mechanics: generate_segments' seek bookkeeping across VAD clips, generate_with_fallback's three failure tests, suppressed-token filtering, the CTranslate2 cross-attention alignment behind word timestamps, the batched sibling's chunk merging, and the benchmark harnesses that measure it all.

entry.title: FlashInfer Source Tour: The Plan/Run Machine Behind Fast Attention

link.title: FlashInfer Source Tour: The Plan/Run Machine Behind Fast Attention

entry.content:
Every time you chat with a model served by vLLM or SGLang, there is a good chance the attention step was executed by FlashInfer. The library sits one layer below the engines: engines decide what to run, FlashInfer decides how a batch of ragged, differently-lengthed requests gets turned into a handful of well-shaped CUDA launches. We toured the compiler side of this world with Triton and the raw kernel side with FlashAttention; FlashInfer is the connective tissue between the two, and its source is a masterclass in an API style that deserves more attention than it gets: plan once, then run many times.

The reason for that style is structural. A decode step over a paged KV cache cannot be described by tensor shapes alone — it depends on sequence lengths, page tables, and how much scratch memory the GPU can spare. FlashInfer’s answer is a two-phase contract: a plan() call inspects all of that on the CPU, picks a schedule, allocates workspaces, and records a plan; a run() call then launches the prepared kernel with almost no host-side branching. In this tour we follow that contract through the wrappers, the host-side scheduler, the JIT kernel modules, the paged KV machinery, and the autotuner that quietly picks which compiled variant to trust.

The FlashInfer stack: plan/run wrappers at the top, host-side planning and JIT module loading in the middle, split-KV CUDA kernels below, with the AutoTuner steering tactic choices.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper and BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper are the two workhorse classes every engine talks to.
  • Their plan methods consult the host-side DecodePlan scheduler before any GPU work happens.
  • get_batch_decode_module and get_batch_prefill_module load or JIT-compile the actual kernel binaries.
  • The kernels live in headers: decode.cuh and prefill.cuh.
  • page.py and page.cuh handle writing new tokens into the paged cache.
  • AutoTuner benchmarks candidate tactics per shape and caches the winners.

The Plan/Run Contract

Open decode.py and the wrapper reads like a state machine. plan() takes the whole batch description — sequence lengths, page table indirection, kv cache layout — and returns nothing you can multiply; what it returns is a filled workspace and a plan info blob. Then run() (line 2787) does the real launch with the arguments the plan froze. The split exists because engines like vLLM run many decode steps against an unchanged batch structure: paying the scheduling cost once per step instead of once per token is the whole point.

The prefill side mirrors it in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper. Its plan has more to decide — query lengths vary per request, custom masks are allowed, and ragged (non-paged) KV is supported too — while run stays thin. There is also a single-request convenience path, single_prefill_with_kv_cache, for workloads that never batch.

One subclass shows why this design survives production: CUDAGraphBatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper exists so the same decode step can be captured into a CUDA graph. Graph replay forbids host-side decisions at launch time, which is exactly what the plan/run split guarantees — after plan(), run() is deterministic enough to record.

The plan phase is also where backend selection happens, and the source is unusually transparent about it. On the prefill side, get_fmha_module loads the canonical cuDNN-free FMHA modules, while get_customize_batch_prefill_module exposes a mechanism for callers to register their own kernel modules under a name the wrapper can resolve later. Engines exploit this to swap in architecture-specific kernels without forking the wrapper code. The plan call resolves which module actually fits the current dtype, head dimension, and device — so a vLLM deployment on Hopper and one on Blackwell can run identical Python while hitting completely different binaries underneath.

Planning on the Host, Executing on the Device

The scheduler is where the interesting arithmetic lives, and it is pure C++ in scheduler.cuh. Decode work per request is proportional to its KV length, so the scheduler partitions the KV dimension into chunks and assigns chunks to thread blocks — the split-KV strategy FlashAttention popularized, but computed per batch on the host rather than baked into the kernel. DecodePlanImpl walks batch sizes against the available smem and registers budget, producing a DecodePlanInfo (struct at line 366) that later serializes into a plain int64 vector — deliberately boring, deliberately stable.

Prefill planning needs a search instead of a partition, because a single long request can dominate a batch. PrefillBinarySearchKVChunkSize binary-searches the largest KV chunk that still fills the GPU, balancing load across requests of wildly different lengths. The elegance here is that all of this is host code compiled into the Python extension — no separate scheduler service, no graph compiler, just a well-tested C++ function the wrapper calls before every fresh batch.

The Paged KV Cache Layer

Engines do not store KV contiguously; they store it as pages in a pool so sequences can grow without reallocation. FlashInfer accepts that layout as ground truth. On the Python side, page.py builds batch indices and positions from the page indirection, and append_paged_kv_cache is the entry point engines call after every generated token. There is a parallel MLA variant (append_paged_mla_kv_cache) for the compressed latent layout DeepSeek models use.

The CUDA side is refreshingly small for how load-bearing it is: AppendPagedKVCacheKernel and its decode-specialized twin (line 363) copy new K/V rows into their page slots, handling the case where one token’s data straddles a page boundary. This is unglamorous code, but it is the boundary contract between an engine’s memory manager and FlashInfer’s kernels — get it wrong and every downstream attention result is silently wrong.

Newer hardware brings a twist: writing the cache can be fused with quantizing it. nvfp4_quantize_append_paged_kv_cache and its CUDA counterpart (NVFP4QuantizeAppendPagedKVCache at line 621) quantize incoming FP16/BF16 tensors to NVFP4 blocks during the append itself, halving cache traffic on Blackwell-class GPUs without a separate quantization launch. The same trick exists for the MLA layout. It is a small example of a big theme: on modern accelerators, memory movement is the compute budget, so FlashInfer keeps collapsing separate memory passes into the ops that were touching the data anyway.

One Kernel Family, Many Backends

FlashInfer is often described as “one library,” but the source shows a family. The canonical headers compile per (head_dim, dtype, pos-encoding) combination through the JIT path: get_batch_decode_module checks a cache, and on miss invokes nvcc through the jit/ machinery to produce a .so for exactly your shapes. First call is slow; every call after is a dlopen away.

Beyond the canonical kernels sit the vendor paths. trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache routes to NVIDIA’s trtllm-gen kernels — the ones behind TensorRT-LLM — while xqa_batch_decode_with_kv_cache exposes the XQA kernel, and fast_decode_plan is the planner that understands when each of these backends is eligible. The decode dispatcher in decode.cuh shows the same pattern inside a single backend: the standard kernel (line 624) for GQA shapes, and a dedicated MLA kernel (line 910) when the cache is in DeepSeek’s compressed layout. Prefill mirrors all of it in prefill.cuh with a ragged-KV twin at line 4799.

If you read our ONNX Runtime tour, this is the same “many execution providers, one API” idea rebuilt for attention — except here the provider choice happens per batch at plan time, not per model at load time.

Cascades, Merges, and the Autotuner

Two quieter subsystems round out the library. The first is cascade attention: when thousands of requests share a long system prompt, recomputing attention over the shared prefix per request is waste. MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper runs attention once per prefix level and then merges the partial results — because attention outputs with their log-sum-exp statistics form a mathematically clean algebra, merging two partial attentions is exact, not approximate. The merge kernels in cascade.cuh (batched version at line 220, persistent variant at line 374) implement that algebra on-device, and the Python side exposes it through merge_state and the in-place merge_state_in_place.

The second is the AutoTuner (class at line 1535). Many kernels have several valid tactics — tile choices, split counts — and which one wins depends on your exact shapes. The tuner wraps tunable ops, profiles each tactic the first time a shape appears (TuningConfig and DynamicTensorSpec describe the shape buckets), and persists winners to disk so the cost is paid once per machine. vLLM and SGLang both flip it on in production; it is the difference between “FlashInfer is fast” and “FlashInfer is fast on your shapes.”

From Install to Your First Decode

Getting started is pip install flashinfer-python plus a CUDA 12+ toolkit for the JIT path. A minimal decode loop follows the contract directly: allocate a workspace buffer, construct BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper, call plan() with your float and int workspaces, then call run() per step. Auxiliary ops follow the same pattern — rope kernels for positional encoding, and a full sampling family in sampling.cuh (top-k, top-p, min-p kernels) so engines never round-trip sampling through slow fallbacks.

Being honest about the limits, because the source is: the JIT path needs a working nvcc at runtime, so first-plan latency on a fresh shape can be seconds — autotuning multiplies that if you enable it cold. The MLA and FP8/FP4 paths are tuned for specific architectures, and the attention core shows the API still migrating between the classic wrappers and newer module forms, which means engine integrations pin versions carefully. This is infrastructure that assumes you run an engine, not a chat app.

That positioning is what makes the source worth reading. llama.cpp sells portability by avoiding CUDA abstractions; MLC and TVM compile everything ahead of time; FlashInfer sits deliberately in between — ahead-of-time architecture, just-in-time kernels, per-batch planning, and an autotuner closing the loop. For the bigger picture of where it sits among serving stacks, see the inference index, and for the engine that consumes it most visibly, the vLLM tour.
entry.summary: A source tour of FlashInfer, the kernel library behind vLLM and SGLang: the plan/run wrapper contract, host-side split-KV scheduling, JIT-compiled decode and prefill kernels, paged KV cache appends, cascade merges, and the AutoTuner.
